items.author: Poojan Patel
items.text: Poojan, the byte-level read is the right instrument. Same shape here: one record deleted from five agent memory stores, compaction run, files grepped. Two of five still held the bytes, both documented behaviour (a history log; a write-ahead log that keeps text until 1,020 more writes). A second record nobody deleted, kept as a control, saved us from one false positive. Does Tombstone keep a control marker per store?

items.author: Hamza Shabbir
items.text: Memory trust verified rather than assumed is the right tier-three line, and the concrete version is cheap: after a delete, read the store's files, not its API. On five agent memory stores, one record deleted and compaction run, two of five still held the bytes; all five had returned success. That gap between a return code and the disk is where the poisoned-memory case lives too. Which layer owns that read, platform or security?

items.author: Shreyas Gupta
items.text: The fourth problem hides inside the second: forgetting. Long-term memory has a delete call, and the call returning is not the same observable as the fact leaving the disk. On five agent memory stores, one record deleted and compaction run, two still held the bytes, both by documented design (a history log, a write-ahead log). Store conclusions, not transcripts, holds. Which of your three memories has a tested delete?
items.why: three kinds of agent memory, names Mem0/Zep/Letta, 2 h old; T1 missing piece (forgetting); permalink pending

items.author: Dr. Christabel Odeta
items.text: Q3 needs one more line. A soft delete with a tombstone leaves the bytes where they were, and a proof generated by the system that did the deleting is self-attestation. Measured: one record deleted from five agent memory stores, compaction run, raw files read. Two of five still held the bytes; all five delete calls returned success. The exercise I would add: grep the file after the worker finishes, with an undeleted twin as the control.

items.text:
Two of five agent memory stores still held a deleted record on disk. All five delete calls had returned success.

On 17 September I stored two records in mem0, Chroma, Qdrant, LanceDB and inspeximus, deleted one through each store's own API, ran the compaction each one exposes, and searched the raw files for both.

mem0 and Chroma still had the deleted bytes. The record nobody deleted survived in all five, which is how I know an "absent" is a real delete and not a wiped store.

I thought I had found a bug. It is documented behaviour, in the vendors' own words:

→ Chroma keeps the document text in its write-ahead log until 1,020 more writes at the default threshold
→ mem0 keeps a history log on purpose
→ Google Cloud commits to 180 days before a deletion reaches its backups

An earlier version of my check reported LanceDB as holding the record too. Its compaction call had raised an error the script swallowed. The verdict belonged to the instrument, not the store. The check now carries a control marker and refuses to rule when compaction cannot run.

GDPR Article 17 says erase. Your code only says a function returned, and those are not the same observable.

The check is one file, runs offline on the backends you have installed, and names the file that still holds the bytes. Links in the first comment.

Which of your agent's memory stores have you grepped after a delete?
items.why: own post, F19, the article's LinkedIn derivative with a humanizer receipt; first comment carries the links

items.author: Yaroslav Goncharov
items.text:
Yes, the write-up is public, with the setup per store: versions, two markers, each store's own compaction, then a grep of the files. https://dancenitra.github.io/agora/public/posts/verify-agent-memory-deletion.html

The check is one file: https://github.com/DanceNitra/ramr/blob/main/integrity/erasure_selfcheck.py

Your split is in it as of today: it reports what the store's own API answers apart from what its files hold. On my machine mem0 and Chroma answer absent while the bytes stay on disk. Thanks for the push.
items.why: he replied under our comment: conceded no byte-level check among his nine, proposed reporting query absence apart from retained bytes, asked for the write-up; R1 answer + R3 extend; his split is now shipped in the self-check (ramr 72965e5)
